ui.title: BOTIA Assistant
ui.welcome: 👋 Hi! I'm the BOTIA assistant. I'll show you things labels don't tell you. You can also ask me anything about ingredients, labels or additives.
ui.limitMessage: You've used your 3 free questions. For unlimited queries, download the BOTIA app.
ui.offTopic: I can only help with questions about food ingredients and labels.
ui.connectionError: Connection error. Please check your network.

questions.text: That appetizing red in your gummy sweets or strawberry yogurt? It's made by crushing thousands of insects.
questions.answer: It's called carmine, or cochineal — E120. It comes from a scale insect farmed on cactus. It's authorised, it's been used for centuries, and it's on more labels than you think.

questions.text: Why do supermarket apples shine like they've been polished?
questions.answer: Shellac (E904) — a resin secreted by an Asian beetle. It seals the fruit and makes it glossy. Fresh fruit doesn't carry an ingredient list, so nobody tells you.

questions.text: Do you know why bagged grated cheese never clumps together?
questions.answer: Cellulose powder — refined wood fibre — is added as an anti-caking agent. It's edible and authorised. It's also not cheese.

questions.text: What has more sugar: a can of soda or four tablespoons of condensed milk?
questions.answer: They're almost tied. But one is sold as a treat and the other under a 'dairy' label. The word on the front changes how you read the same amount of sugar.

questions.text: You think jarred tomato sauce is just tomato and oil?
questions.answer: In most brands sugar sits near the top of the ingredient list — added to cut the acidity. Ingredients are listed by weight, so its position tells you how much is in there.

questions.text: A '0% fat' yogurt sounds good. But what replaces the fat so it still feels creamy?
questions.answer: Usually modified starch or maltodextrin. Fat carries texture and flavour — take it out and something has to do that job instead.

questions.text: Is your brown bread actually wholemeal, or white bread wearing a costume?
questions.answer: Colour proves nothing. Bran or malt can darken white flour. The only way to know is the ingredient list — wholemeal flour has to be first.

questions.text: Did you know white chocolate contains no cocoa solids at all?
questions.answer: It's cocoa butter, milk and sugar. The fat from the bean, not the bean. Legally it's chocolate. Botanically it's barely related.

questions.text: Why does carton juice taste identical in January and in August?
questions.answer: It's stored for months in oxygen-free tanks, which strips the aroma. Flavour packs are added back before bottling. Same fruit, reassembled.

questions.text: 'With natural flavouring' on a lemon biscuit. Does it come from a lemon?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. 'Natural' describes the source being natural, not which one. It can come from a fungus, bark or fermentation, and the label never says.

questions.text: Do you buy brown sugar because it feels more natural?
questions.answer: Most supermarket brown sugar is refined white sugar with molasses added back for colour. Your body treats it the same. You're paying for the tint.

questions.text: How can cured meat claim 'no artificial preservatives' and still last a month?
questions.answer: Celery extract. It's naturally rich in nitrates, which turn into the same nitrites the label is avoiding naming. Natural source, identical chemistry.

questions.text: Almost every tin in your cupboard has a plastic lining inside.
questions.answer: Many have used BPA, which mimics oestrogen in the body. Some brands have moved away from it. The tin doesn't tell you which.

questions.text: 'Microwave safe' on a plastic container. Safe for what, exactly?
questions.answer: It means the plastic won't melt or warp. It says nothing about what migrates into your food when it heats up.

questions.text: Cling film on cheese and cling film on lettuce are not the same thing.
questions.answer: Plasticisers dissolve into fat. Wrap something fatty and migration goes up sharply. Wrap something watery and it barely moves.

questions.text: That water bottle you left in the car in August.
questions.answer: Heat degrades PET. It releases antimony and microplastics into the water. If it tastes faintly of plastic, that's not your imagination.

questions.text: Gelatine has no flavour, no colour and no smell. So where does it come from?
questions.answer: Collagen, extracted from animal skin and bone. It's in sweets, yogurts, capsules and mousses. The word gives nothing away.

questions.text: Why doesn't the oil separate in your mayonnaise, ever?
questions.answer: Emulsifiers like E471 hold water and fat together against their nature. Left alone they'd separate in minutes.

questions.text: Xanthan gum is in your sauce, your gluten-free bread and your ice cream.
questions.answer: It's produced by fermenting sugar with a bacterium. A tiny amount thickens a whole batch. It's one of the most widely used texture ingredients there is.

questions.text: Some plant milks contain an ingredient extracted from red seaweed.
questions.answer: Carrageenan. It stops the drink separating on the shelf. It's authorised, and it's also under active scientific review for its effects on the gut.

questions.text: Sucralose is around 600 times sweeter than sugar.
questions.answer: That's why you only need milligrams. It's made by modifying sugar itself, replacing three parts of the molecule so the body doesn't process it.

questions.text: Why do sugar-free sweets sometimes come with a warning about digestion?
questions.answer: Sugar alcohols like maltitol and sorbitol aren't fully absorbed. What isn't absorbed keeps going, and in quantity that has consequences.

questions.text: Stevia on the front of the pack. Steviol glycosides in the ingredients.
questions.answer: The sweetener is an extracted compound from the leaf, purified in a lab — not the plant itself. The picture of a green leaf is doing a lot of work.

questions.text: In 2022 the EU banned a whitening agent that the US still allows.
questions.answer: Titanium dioxide, E171. EFSA concluded it could no longer be considered safe. Same substance, same evidence, two different answers.

questions.text: The same additive can be E471 here, INS 471 internationally and something else entirely in the US.
questions.answer: Three naming systems for one substance. Manufacturers know exactly what each code means. That's the gap BOTIA exists to close.

questions.text: Lecithin is what stops chocolate turning grainy.
questions.answer: It's an emulsifier, and it's usually from soy or sunflower. But the label doesn't always say which — and it can also be from egg.

questions.text: 'Trans fat free' doesn't always mean zero.
questions.answer: In many places a product can round down to zero below a certain threshold per portion. Eat three portions and the maths changes.

questions.text: Ingredients are listed by weight, from most to least.
questions.answer: So the first three tell you what the product actually is. If sugar is second, the rest of the front label is decoration.

questions.text: Real food doesn't need flavourings.
questions.answer: When a label lists added flavour, it means processing stripped the original taste and it had to be put back. That's one of NOVA's markers for ultra-processed food.

questions.text: A product can be low in sugar, low in fat, high in protein — and still be ultra-processed.
questions.answer: NOVA doesn't classify by nutrients. It classifies by whether the ingredient list contains substances you'd never find in a kitchen.

questions.text: Fruit juice concentrate is used to sweeten products that say 'no added sugar'.
questions.answer: WHO counts it as a free sugar. Concentrating fruit removes the water and the fibre — what's left behaves like syrup.

questions.text: Glycerol appears in sweets, drinks and baked goods — and it can be animal or plant.
questions.answer: The label rarely says which. Same name, same code, two completely different origins.

questions.text: Food enzymes are used in bread, cheese and juice — and often don't appear on the label at all.
questions.answer: In many cases they're treated as processing aids, not ingredients. Which means they legally don't have to be declared.

questions.text: Large predatory fish concentrate mercury from everything they eat.
questions.answer: Methylmercury accumulates up the food chain. That's why advice on swordfish and tuna differs from advice on sardines.

questions.text: Some compounds don't leave the body — they settle in fat and wait.
questions.answer: Lipophilic substances accumulate over years and release during rapid weight loss, pregnancy or menopause, in concentrated form.

questions.text: BHA and BHT keep fats from going rancid in crisps, cereals and chewing gum.
questions.answer: Both are under scientific review for possible hormonal activity. Both are still authorised. Both are on labels right now.

questions.text: Parabens are known as cosmetics ingredients — but they also appear in food.
questions.answer: They're used as preservatives, and they're studied for endocrine activity. The cosmetics debate and the food one are the same substance.

questions.text: Cadmium gets into food through the soil, not the factory.
questions.answer: Plants absorb it from contaminated ground. It's in cocoa, shellfish and some cereals — and no ingredient list will ever mention it.

questions.text: Aspartame is one of the most studied food additives in history.
questions.answer: Thousands of papers, decades of review, and the debate is still open. That's not a scandal — that's what an unsettled question looks like.

questions.text: Erythritol passes through the body almost untouched.
questions.answer: That's why it has almost no calories. Around 90% is absorbed and excreted unchanged, which is also why it's gentler on digestion than other sugar alcohols.

questions.text: WHO advised in 2023 against using non-sugar sweeteners for weight control.
questions.answer: Not because they're unsafe, but because long-term use showed no benefit for weight — and possible associations with other risks.

questions.text: Guar gum comes from a bean grown mostly in India.
questions.answer: It thickens at cold temperatures, which is why it's in ice cream and cold sauces. A crop failure there changes prices worldwide.

questions.text: Konjac is a root used to make noodles with almost no calories.
questions.answer: It's nearly all fibre and water. It's also been restricted in some jelly products because of how it behaves when swallowed whole.

questions.text: Vinegar seems like the simplest ingredient on a label.
questions.answer: It's produced by fermenting alcohol. Which is why what looks obvious isn't always obvious to everyone reading the label.

questions.text: Lead in food doesn't come from an ingredient. It comes from everything around it.
questions.answer: Soil, water, old pipes, some ceramics. It's a contaminant, not an additive — which is exactly why the label can't warn you.

questions.text: Some ingredients can be animal, plant or alcohol-based, and the label looks identical either way.
questions.answer: E471, lecithins, enzymes, gelatine, glycerol, natural flavourings. In BOTIA's first analysis, 72% of products couldn't be confirmed either way.

questions.text: Saccharin was discovered in 1879 by a chemist who forgot to wash his hands.
questions.answer: He noticed his bread tasted sweet. It's been through bans, warnings and reinstatements since — and it's still on shelves today.

questions.text: Cyclamates are banned in the United States and authorised in the European Union.
questions.answer: Same substance, same science, opposite conclusions. Regulation is not a single global truth.

questions.text: Dioxins aren't added to anything. They're a by-product of combustion.
questions.answer: They settle on grass, animals eat it, and they concentrate in fat and dairy. Nothing on a label can tell you they're there.

questions.text: Nutritional labelling was never designed to show how processed something is.
questions.answer: It counts nutrients. It cannot see reformulation. The ingredient list can — but it was never meant to be read as a whole.
